paras: The attack on James Thompson at the Savannah polls was an attempt by a crowd of about 200 Black men to kill Thompson, a Black voter, at a polling place in Savannah, Georgia, on election day in November 1888. According to a wire dispatch, Thompson was targeted because he was 'found voting the Democratic ticket'; he escaped to a nearby office, police and constabulary drove the crowd back, and the ringleaders were arrested. Papers from Virginia to Dakota printed the story among their election-day news.

Thompson, described as 'a colored man', lived six miles outside Savannah and walked into the city to vote. The two earliest printings date the dispatch November 6, while a Dakota paper two days later dated it November 7.

At the polls a crowd that the dispatch put at 200 'negroes' surrounded Thompson and, in the wire's words, 'endeavored to take the life of' him. A 'knot of white men' protected him and hustled him away from the polling place. He took refuge in the office of Julian Schley, six blocks from the voting place, and the crowd surrounded the building. Police and constabulary then beat the crowd back.
The dispatch said that the ringleaders were arrested but gave no names or charges. No report of a hearing, trial or later account appears in the coverage, and no injury to Thompson is mentioned.

All known coverage comes from a single wire dispatch, and the four printings differ mainly in their headlines. The Richmond Daily Times ran it on November 7 as 'Negro Bulldozers in the South', casting the crowd as Black election intimidators, while the Wilmington Daily Republican the same day chose 'Trying to Kill a Democratic Negro'. On November 9 the Mitchell Capital in Dakota headed it 'Mobbed by Negroes' with the subhead 'A Colored Man Attacked Because He Voted a Democratic Ticket', placing it among other election-day briefs.

The Charlotte Messenger printed a shortened version without a headline in its November 10 election returns, saying the crowd was 'kept back' rather than 'beaten back' by the police. None of the printings carried comment beyond the headlines, and no Savannah paper's own account was found.

reader.title: Attack on James Thompson at the Savannah polls
bases: An election-day crowd tried to kill a man for how he voted but was driven off before anyone was reported hurt, so this was an attempted attack, not a killing (A1, A2, A3).

A crowd of about 200 tried to kill Thompson, with no lawful authority, but police drove it back and no death or injury is reported; the stated motive was his Democratic vote, a political reason rather than a claim of justice (A1, A2, A3).
All four papers print one wire dispatch with nearly the same wording, and no local Savannah or independent account was found (A1, A2, A3, A4).

accounts.label: Wire report from Savannah
accounts.gist: A crowd of 200 Black men tried to kill Thompson for voting Democratic; white men got him away to Schley's office, where police and constabulary beat back the crowd and arrested the ringleaders.

framing.detail: The Richmond Daily Times headed the dispatch 'Negro Bulldozers in the South', presenting the crowd as Black election intimidators.
The Wilmington Daily Republican headed it 'Trying to Kill a Democratic Negro'.
The Mitchell Capital ran it as 'Mobbed by Negroes. A Colored Man Attacked Because He Voted a Democratic Ticket' among other election-day briefs.
The Charlotte Messenger ran a shortened, unheaded paragraph inside its election returns.

conflicts.note: The two papers that printed the story on Nov. 7 carry a Nov. 6 dateline, so the Nov. 7 dateline in the later Dakota printing looks like a re-dating of the wire; Nov. 6 is the better-supported date.

record_check.dossier: 1888-11-06: the two earliest printings (Nov. 7) carry a Nov. 6 dateline; only the Nov. 9 Dakota printing says Nov. 7
mob_assault: an election-day crowd attack in which no one was reported killed or hurt
